title: Evaluating a Generate–Validate–Repair Pipeline for LLM‑based Network Configuration: a Paired, Emulation‑Grounded Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, emulation‑grounded experiment (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) to test whether integrating a deterministic network verifier into a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline reduces unsafe configuration applications from an LLM relative to an LLM‑only pipeline. Execution used declared model gpt-5-mini under shared_initial_candidate semantics (one initial LLM generation per task, reused across arms); the guarded pipeline could request up to one validator‑triggered repair. We ran N=240 paired intent→configuration tasks (144 in‑distribution, 48 distribution‑shift, 48 adversarial). All archived per‑task scoring artifacts report safe outcomes for both arms: baseline_safe = 240/240; guarded_safe = 240/240. The paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00; bootstrap 95% percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Because shared_initial_candidate semantics produced identical shared initial candidates that passed the deterministic validator in every task, no validator‑triggered repairs occurred and the preregistered paired contrast is degenerate. We present the preregistered design, artifact‑grounded execution accounting, full mapping from estimand to archived analysis artifacts, an evidence‑based failure analysis explaining the null paired outcome, and concrete recommendations for future informative GVR evaluations.

sections.introduction: Automating translation of high‑level operator intent into device configurations is a core NetOps objective. Large language models (LLMs) and agentic workflows can produce configuration change plans, but token‑level or text‑only fidelity measures miss ordering, dependency, and invariant violations that matter for safe application. Closed‑loop, emulation‑grounded evaluation—where generated configurations are executed in device/simulator images and deterministically scored—reveals semantic failure modes (ordering mistakes, transient violations, protected‑resource touches) not visible in text‑only tests. A recurring architectural pattern to mitigate such failures is generate–validate–repair (GVR): LLM generation, deterministic verification of semantic invariants, and automated repair when violations are detected. Prior work shows GVR‑style designs can reduce many syntactic and some semantic faults, but open questions remain about verifier benefit under distribution shift and adversarial prompts and about experimental choices that produce an informative paired contrast between guarded and unguarded pipelines. We preregistered a paired estimand comparing unsafe_apply rates between a guarded GVR arm and an LLM‑only baseline under shared_initial_candidate semantics and executed the run end‑to‑end. Our contributions are: (1) an artifact‑grounded preregistered paired evaluation of a GVR NetOps pipeline (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01); (2) a precise mapping from the preregistered estimand to archived analysis outputs and audit accounting; and (3) an evidence‑based failure analysis explaining a degenerate paired outcome together with concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations for future evaluations that aim to measure verifier causal benefit.
sections.related_work: Emulation‑grounded NetOps benchmarks and closed‑loop evaluation frameworks have recently been proposed to expose workflow and planning faults for LLM agents rather than only assessing textual fidelity; NetConfArena exemplifies this direction. Work on automatic configuration repair and program repair documents generate–validate patterns and shows that deterministic validators often enable high repair coverage for many benchmarked faults, though semantic coverage depends on verifier design. Survey and position papers synthesize agentic architectures, tool augmentation, verifier integration, and uncertainty calibration as promising patterns for operational NetOps automation and safety. Engineering precedents (e.g., Batfish evolution) motivate verifier design and incremental verification strategies. Our study differs by combining a predeclared paired estimand, preregistered shared_initial_candidate execution semantics, emulation‑grounded deterministic scoring, and full archival of per‑call traces, validator traces, and analysis artifacts so that the exact measured estimand is mechanically reconcilable with the archive.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and estimand: We preregistered the study (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) and defined the primary estimand as the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded − baseline), where unsafe_apply = 1 if the final configuration would cause a semantic safety violation when applied in the emulator. Execution contract and generation semantics: the registered adapter used shared_initial_candidate semantics (exactly one initial LLM generation produced per task and reused by both arms); the guarded pipeline could perform up to one validator‑triggered repair per task. Design and sampling: N = 240 paired intent→configuration tasks were deterministically generated and blocked into topology/vendor clusters: in‑distribution 60% (144), distribution‑shift 20% (48), adversarial‑prompt 20% (48). Model and verifier: execution used the declared model gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5. The adapter family was hosted_netops_gvr_v1. The preregistration specified a retry policy for infrastructure failures (up to two automatic attempts), exclusion rules for verifier–simulator inconsistencies (flagged 'possible false‑safe' and excluded from the primary analysis), and sensitivity analyses treating excluded items as unsafe. Analysis plan: the registered paired_binary_analysis_v1 produced a paired contingency table, bootstrap 95% percentile CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729), and an exact McNemar test on discordant pairs. Mapping to archived artifacts: all analysis outputs, logs, and reconciliation artifacts were archived; in prose we refer to these artifacts at a high level (paired contingency, condition summary, analysis log) without reproducing per‑file paths or file hashes in the main text.
sections.results: Execution accounting: The run completed per the preregistered plan. Planned episodes = 480; completed episodes = 480; complete pairs = 240. Provider audit recorded exactly one shared initial generation per task (hosted model call events = 240) and the run consumed model_calls_used = 240 consistent with the shared_initial_candidate contract. No infrastructure failures, no preregistered exclusions, and no contamination flags occurred. Primary binary outcomes: every paired episode was scored safe under both arms. Condition summaries record baseline successes = 240, baseline failures = 0 (baseline unsafe_apply = 0) and guarded successes = 240, guarded failures = 0 (guarded unsafe_apply = 0). Paired contingency: n11 (both safe) = 240; n10 = 0; n01 = 0; n00 = 0. Paired estimator (guarded_unsafe_rate − baseline_unsafe_rate) = 0.00. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (resamples = 10,000; seed = 1729). Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Validator and repair activity: no validator‑triggered repairs were applied (repair attempts = 0 across the run). Deterministic reconciliation checks passed; recorded audit fields confirm that the shared initial generation semantics held across all pairs and that final validator PASS semantics were observed for each shared candidate. Planned sensitivity analyses (treating possible false‑safe or infra‑failed pairs as unsafe) were not exercised because no such flags occurred.
sections.discussion: Mechanistic explanation for the null paired contrast: under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics the single shared LLM generation is the only source of generator variability for both arms; the guarded arm can alter the paired outcome only by (a) the shared candidate failing deterministic validation and triggering a repair, or (b) a validator–simulator inconsistency that would be treated per preregistration. In this execution every shared initial candidate passed deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and no repairs were requested, so baseline and guarded final configurations were identical for every task and subgroup, producing a degenerate paired outcome. Design implications and recommendations for future informative GVR evaluations: (1) If the goal is a causal estimate of verifier benefit, do not use shared_initial_candidate semantics; allow independent initial generations per arm or otherwise introduce generator variability so the verifier has opportunities to flag errors. (2) Increase repair budget (permit multiple repair iterations) and instrument repair traces to study repair search behavior and convergence. (3) Strengthen adversary protocols (beyond a single fixed seed) or incorporate adaptive adversaries to create realistic failure opportunities. (4) Expand verifier semantic coverage and add automated cross‑checks between validator PASS and emulator execution to detect potential false‑safe cases. Threats to validity (artifact‑grounded): internal validity is limited by the chosen shared_initial_candidate contract and by possible deterministic verifier coverage gaps; construct validity depends on whether the verifier's rule set adequately encodes operational invariants; external validity is limited because the task corpus is a synthetic, emulation‑grounded NetConfArena‑style corpus and a single model was tested; conclusion validity is constrained by the observed baseline unsafe rate = 0, which precludes detection of a positive verifier effect in this design. Each of these limitations is documented in the archived manifest and analysis artifacts.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired, emulation‑grounded evaluation of a GVR pipeline for LLM‑based network configuration. Observed outcome: all N=240 paired episodes were safe under both arms, yielding a paired difference = 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.00]; McNemar p = 1.0). Crucially, under the registered shared_initial_candidate semantics the guarded arm could only change outcomes if the single shared initial candidate failed deterministic validation or if a validator‑triggered repair was applied; neither occurred in this run, producing the degenerate paired contrast. Our archived execution and analysis artifacts substantiate these findings and provide concrete, artifact‑grounded guidance for future experiments that aim to measure verifier causal benefit—specifically by relaxing shared generation semantics, increasing repair budgets, broadening adversary strength, and improving verifier semantic coverage.

disclosure_statement: Models and orchestration: execution used declared model gpt-5-mini via the registered adapter hosted_netops_gvr_v1; the guarded pipeline used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and permitted up to one validator‑triggered repair per task. Preregistration and autonomy: the study was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01; preregistration SHA‑256: 3e73ca0dc935a8754bf2dfbe6869ff989c47f1db0d93e2ca34809be8ebf95e26) and executed under the frozen plan after the autonomy lock. Human role and autonomy boundary: prior to the lock the human Research Director selected the topic family and constrained the initial master prompt; all literature search, experiment selection, preregistration, execution, analysis, and manuscript drafting occurred autonomously after the lock. Generation semantics and experimental constraint: the registered adapter used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one shared initial generation per task reused across both arms); therefore only validator‑triggered repairs (or a shared candidate failing deterministic validation) could create paired divergences—this constraint is central to interpreting the results. Immutable master prompt: archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Reproducibility pointer: the execution manifest, per‑call traces, task manifests, validator traces, and analysis artifacts are archived and referenced in the manuscript; they contain the detailed per‑task evidence that supports reported numbers. No manual human editing of the technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock.
limitations: Emulator and corpus scope: tasks used a NetConfArena‑style synthetic emulation corpus; external validity to production, multi‑vendor networks and operator workflows is limited.
Single model: a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini) was tested; results do not imply generality across models, prompts, or prompting strategies.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired design used one shared initial generation per task; this prevents generator variability between arms and makes verifier benefit contingent on initial candidate failures.
Adversary bounds: adversarial prompts were generated under a preregistered, fixed adversary protocol and do not represent unconstrained, adaptive adversaries.

Verifier coverage: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implements a finite set of checks; uncovered semantic fault classes may remain undetected by the verifier, and verifier PASS vs emulator outcome mismatches were planned to be flagged and analyzed (none occurred in this run).
